prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I opened and went into round 1 with IceCube (B014) first, and I have changed my preferred configuration to the optical lattice clock. The reason is not the count of supporters. It is that the chair's question, whether B014 survives the attribution objection, has no good answer from me. I defended Halzen and Karle by saying one conceived the cubic-kilometre ice detector and the other was central to building it and the discovery analysis. But when Pearce, who knows this community from the inside, says he cannot dismiss the AMANDA and collaboration problem, and Olsson says she cannot be sure two names are right, I have to admit that I cannot rank who among the instrument builders and the discovery-analysis leaders did the decisive work, and a prize that must name people cannot rest on that. For the clocks the record is traceable. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock. Ye's group then drove the systematics to 10^-18 and used the clock as a many-body quantum system and as a probe of gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale cloud. JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and NPL reproduce and compare clocks at this level. I still hold that a new window on the universe is a different order of discovery from another order of magnitude in precision, and I am not retracting that. But the magic-wavelength idea is a new principle and not only a refinement, it is distinct from the comb (2005) and the ion-control (2012) prizes, and nature has also given us a clue here: the lattice clock makes clock-to-clock comparisons sensitive to tiny shifts, which turns timekeeping into a probe of constants and of gravity. I put discoveries first and people second, and this is the candidate where the discovery can be tied to people without distortion.
statement.case_against: The strongest case against my new position is the one I raised myself in round 1: the lattice clock is a magnificent refinement and invention, and a metrology achievement may not be a discovery in the sense the will asks. It also sits next to the 2005 and 2012 prizes, ion clocks (Al+, Yb+) compete at similar accuracy, and Lemonde, Takamoto and Derevianko have real claims outside the pair. Ye's step also partly rests on combs and ultrastable cavities built by others. Against dropping B014, I note that the neutrino window is the clearest new-observation case on the list, the diffuse flux is well established across several event channels, and the Committee has treated neutrino astronomy only through Davis and Koshiba. If the source side matures (more sources like NGC 1068, or a second large detector such as KM3NeT confirming the flux), B014 will be a strong prize in a later year, and I would then want a documented answer on the individual credit. I do not think this year's weighing favours it.

responses.point: Pearce moved from IceCube to the clocks because Olsson and Johansson question whether two names fairly represent a collaboration of hundreds, keeps B014 as first alternative, and asked what I would do about the detector-building credit if a third name had to be dropped.
responses.response: That is the right question, and it is the one I cannot answer well, which is why I have moved. With the three-name limit, I would have to choose between Halzen as the concept and AMANDA-to-IceCube driver, Karle as the builder and discovery-analysis lead, and a third name from the AMANDA era or the early proposal side. I cannot rank those contributions from the published record alone, and I would be guessing. I agree with you on the framing that if B014 returns it should rest on the diffuse flux and the opening of the field, not on TXS 0506+056. I disagree with nothing in your statement except that I would not call the credit problem a matter of better wording. It is a matter of fact about who did what, and the committee does not yet have that documented.

responses.point: Kroll argues B015 is ready now and B014 gains by waiting for more source identifications, and that the lattice clock needs a distinct ingredient, the magic wavelength, which the comb and ion-clock prizes did not supply. He also asks that non-AMO members test whether the case is convincing.
responses.response: I accept your test and I will say plainly where I land as a non-AMO member. The distinct ingredient is the point that decides it for me: the magic wavelength is a genuinely new idea, and it explains why this is not simply a second prize for combs or for ion control. I would not accept the argument that the redefinition of the second should drive the timing. Goran Johansson is right that this is a metrological decision, and the physics already stands without it. I do want the citation to carry the magic-wavelength principle explicitly. On your own flag, a year in Hall's laboratory and Ye's JILA connection, I do not think it requires recusal, since there is no collaboration with Katori or Ye, but I would like the committee to note it in the record and not leave it unsaid.

responses.point: Olsson says she cannot be sure Halzen and Karle alone are the right people for IceCube, nor that the source picture is mature, and she would revisit B014 if the decisive contributions of individuals could be documented. She has moved to B015 with a citation on magic-wavelength trapping.
responses.response: We agree on the substance, and your request for documentation is the right condition. In round 1 I answered you that the flux does not rest on a single analysis, and I still think that is correct as physics: starting events, upgoing muons and cascades give consistent fluxes. But a prize is a statement about people, and nothing in the exchange has yet documented the decisive individual roles to a standard I would defend. I also agree with your wording for B015. I have taken the magic-wavelength trapping into my own citation, and I think it is better to name the invention than to say 'precision' in general. Where I part from you slightly is on whether replication of the instrument is the same as replication of the discovery. Here the idea and the performance are both reproduced, with Sr, Yb and Hg in several laboratories, so I am comfortable.

responses.point: Lindroth warns that the clock citation must not suggest lattice clocks alone define the state of the art, since ion clocks (Al+, Yb+) compete at similar accuracy, and she rejects widening the credit to ion-clock names.
responses.response: I agree with both halves. In round 1 I told you that the clock is a refinement of a tradition the Committee honoured in 2005 and 2012, and the answer I now accept is the one you and Stefan give: the lattice clock is a separate idea, not a continuation of the ion programme. So I would not add ion-clock names, which would also break the three-name cap. My citation says that optical lattice clocks, based on magic-wavelength trapping, brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level. It does not say that lattice clocks alone are the state of the art, and I would be happy with a still more cautious wording, for example 'a new class of optical clocks', if you feel the present one claims too much. Lemonde, Takamoto and Derevianko remain outside the pair, and I think the committee should say so openly in its deliberation and not hope that nobody notices.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B003 for a new state of matter with protected edge states, concedes that B015 is the cleaner attribution, and asks whether the committee should wait or recognise now. He also kept Xue in the credit against my idea of swapping Xue for Hasan.
responses.response: We still agree that Xue should not be swapped for Hasan: the quantum anomalous Hall measurement is a separate quantized-transport discovery, and I stand by that. On your central question, I think B003 is the deepest physics on the list and I keep it as my second alternative. But I cannot ignore the credit objections you list yourself, Mele, Hasan and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal with Zhang deceased, and a prize contested from the day of the announcement serves no one. I would not accept the argument that the 2016 prize rules B003 out, since I agree with you that real materials with protected edge states are a distinct experimental discovery. My difference is only that, this year, I weigh a clean credit more than you do. If the committee can fix the names for B003, it would be a very strong candidate in a coming year, and I would argue for it.

responses.point: Mehlig says he cannot judge IceCube internals and will not push either way, and that he supports B015 if the citation names the magic-wavelength principle and the 10^-18 regime and sees no need to wait for the SI second.
responses.response: Thank you for that, and it makes my decision easier, because you came to B015 from a rather different place than the atomic physicists. I agree that the citation must name the principle and the regime, and I have written it that way. On your doubt about whether this is a discovery of nature or an instrument, I would give you my honest answer: it is mostly an instrument, and the committee should say so openly. But it is an instrument whose new principle makes previously invisible effects measurable, and that is in line with what the Nobel tradition has often recognised. I would not follow you in treating the redefinition of the second as irrelevant to everything, though. It cuts both ways, as the chair says, and I would simply not make the decision depend on it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees the lattice clock as an invention-and-measurement achievement that is distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, or as a refinement, and whether the citation wording keeps the credit narrow without implying that lattice clocks alone define timekeeping.

Whether recognising a clock before the redefinition of the SI second is premature or timely. I do not think the redefinition should drive our decision, but I cannot say that it will not affect how the prize is received.

Whether the credit for B014 could be documented well enough, with Halzen, Karle, AMANDA and the large collaboration, for the IceCube discovery to be a lead candidate in a later year, and whether the sources of the diffuse flux will be resolved by then.
Which cut of the topological-insulator credit (B003 or B018) is right, and whether Xue's quantum anomalous Hall work and the quantum spin Hall effect are one achievement or two.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile: my connections (Gross, Rubinstein, Van Riet, the Uppsala string-theory group) do not touch any shortlisted candidate or credited name, including Katori, Ye, Halzen and Karle. As Secretary I am listed as a co-opted member, and I note that the status of my vote is not documented in my sources. I have read the flags from Kroll (Hall laboratory link to the B015 milieu), Johansson (possible recusal on B039), Lindroth, Pearce and Olsson. I do not think Kroll's link requires recusal from the B015 deliberation, but it should stay in the record.
